summary: A reference guide giving a bibliographic summary of the RFCs numbered 1 through 999, issued from 1969 to 1987. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It is a library catalog for the first thousand Internet memos, listing each one so you can find what you need.

where to find bibliography of rfc 1 to 999
subtitle: A complete bibliographic guide to nearly a thousand Internet memos from the first two decades.

tldr.problem: By 1987, RFC 1000 had been reached and the series was too large for any single reader to navigate by memory. Researchers needed a complete reference to understand which RFCs existed, who wrote them, when they were published, and what they covered.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1012 provides a bibliographic entry for each RFC from 1 through 999: author(s), title, RFC number, NIC registry number (if one exists), organization, and publication date. Entries follow standard bibliographic format, making the document both a reference guide and an index.
tldr.outcome: It became the standard reference for locating and citing early RFCs, and serves historians and protocol engineers as a comprehensive map of the first eighteen years of Internet development.

today: RFC 1012 remains the authoritative bibliographic reference for RFCs 1-999. Many RFCs it lists have been obsoleted; others remain standards. The document itself is Informational, not a standard. However, it is an invaluable historical record and a practical tool for anyone needing to verify or cite an early RFC.

sections.title: The Complete Bibliographic Record
sections.content:
RFC 1012 is a reference guide providing bibliographic information for RFCs 1 through 999, issued between 1969 and 1987. Unlike RFC 800 or RFC 899, which provide annotated summaries and notes, RFC 1012 is a pure bibliographic listing: for each RFC, you get the number, the author or authors, the title in quotes, the RFC and NIC registry numbers, the organization, and the date.

This comprehensive format makes RFC 1012 invaluable for researchers, historians, and standards implementers. If you need to know whether an RFC exists, who wrote it, when it was published, or how to cite it, RFC 1012 is your first stop.
sections.eli5: This book lists every Internet memo from number 1 to 999. For each one, it says who wrote it, what the title is, and when they wrote it. Think of it as the library card catalog for the Internet's first eighteen years.

sections.title: Scope and Coverage: 1969-1987
sections.content:
RFC 1 (Steve Crocker's "Host Software", April 7, 1969) is the oldest. RFC 999 appears in the document listing but is noted as "Status of Prior RFCs". In between are 998 documents spanning nearly two decades of networking research and development. A few RFCs were never issued (RFC 14, 26, 92, 853 are marked as "Never Issued"), and a few others like RFC 17a are variants or supplements, showing how the RFC series evolved to accommodate discussions and clarifications.

The document lists RFCs from the ARPANET era (1969-1974), the NCP-to-TCP transition (1974-1983), and the early Internet period (1983-1987). Each period brought different kinds of documents: early memos on network protocols and implementation, transition planning documents, standards specifications, operational reports, and policy statements. RFC 1012 captures this entire arc in one systematic listing.
sections.eli5: These 999 papers span from 1969 to 1987. They start with the very first ideas about networking, go through a big changeover from one protocol system to another, and end with the Internet becoming the main system. Some of the papers were never finished (they're marked 'Never Issued').

sections.title: How It's Organized and What Each Entry Contains
sections.content:
RFC 1012 lists RFCs in numerical order. Each entry follows a standard format: number, author(s), title (in quotes), RFC number (redundant with the entry number but useful for cross-reference), NIC registry number when applicable, the author's organization, and publication date. For example, RFC 1 reads: "Crocker, Steve, 'Host Software', RFC 1 (NIC 4687), UCLA/NMC, 7 April 1969."

This bibliographic format is readable for humans and structured enough for automated processing. It shows at a glance whether an RFC has an associated NIC number (Network Information Center, where early RFCs were registered), which organization produced it, and when. Multi-author RFCs list all authors in order. Notes on "Never Issued" or variant numbers appear inline, so readers know when an RFC slot was skipped or a variant was issued.
sections.eli5: Each line says: the number, who wrote it, the title in quotes, another way to find it (the NIC number), where they worked, and what date they published it. If a paper was never finished, it just says 'Never Issued' instead.

sections.title: What the Listing Reveals About Internet Evolution
sections.content:
Reading through RFC 1012 in sequence, you see the evolution of concerns and technologies. Early RFCs (1-100) discuss basic protocols and network topology. The 100-200 range covers Telnet development and refinement. The 200-400 range introduces file transfer protocols, mail systems, and network management. By 500, core standards like TCP and IP are stable; discussion shifts to optimization, extensibility, and deployment at scale.

The authors also evolve: early RFCs cluster at UCLA, MIT, Stanford, BBN, and SRI. As the network grows, more organizations contribute. Some individuals (Steve Crocker, Jon Postel, Vint Cerf) appear frequently, suggesting their leadership in protocol design. By the 900s, the RFC series is truly international, with contributions from CCITT, ISO, and diverse academic and research institutions. RFC 1012 thus serves as an organizational and social history of the Internet's development.
sections.eli5: If you read through this list from start to end, you can see how the Internet work changed. At first, a few people at four universities were designing everything. By 1987, thousands of people from around the world were involved. The early papers are about basic ideas; later ones are about refinements and optimization.

sections.title: Using RFC 1012 as a Reference
sections.content:
RFC 1012 serves multiple purposes. For a researcher encountering an RFC number in a paper or documentation, it allows quick lookup: does RFC 700 exist? Who wrote it? When? For authors or standards bodies, it provides the correct bibliographic format for citing RFCs, ensuring consistency. For historians, it offers a complete chronological record of what was documented and when.

The document is organized by RFC number (not by topic or author), so you need to know the RFC number to look it up. For topic-based searching, RFC 800 and RFC 899 with their annotations remain more helpful. But for comprehensive verification and citation, RFC 1012 is definitive.
sections.eli5: If someone mentions an old RFC and you want to know if it's real, when it came out, and who wrote it, you can look it up here. It also tells you the official way to write the citation so people know what you're talking about.
